neighbours.label: the first digit of a metric figure in brackets converted from pounds or nautical miles, e.g. '(4' in '90 pounds (41 kg)', for first digits 2, 4 and 7
fire: The otter can weigh 50 pounds (23 kilograms) in late summer.
The patrol boat stayed 150 nautical miles (278 km) from the shore.
An adult male reaches 100 pounds (45 kilograms) by its third year.
The freighter was spotted 40 nautical miles (74 km) south of the cape.
The sack on the scale came to 95 pounds (43 kilograms) that morning.
The convoy turned back 130 nautical miles (241 km) from the port.
The young seal was about 60 pounds (27 kilograms) when it was tagged.
The radar can track planes 25 nautical miles (46 km) from the tower.
quiet: The otter can weigh 50 pounds or so in late summer, and more after.
The patrol road stayed 30 miles (48 km) from the shore.
An adult male reaches 15 miles (24 km) in a day during its third year.
The freighter was spotted just south of the cape (see the chart).
The sack on the scale came to 95 pounds that morning (we checked).
The convoy turned back 200 feet (61 metres) from the bridge.
The young seal (the smaller one) was about 60 pounds when it was tagged.
The road runs 45 miles (72 km) from the tower to the coast.

short: first digit of a hard conversion
notes: Conversions from miles or feet stay near zero, though the first digits are the same kind; first digit 1 goes to the + pole. Why these units differ is open.
